title: Why Autonomous Medical Coding and CDI Must Operate As One Workflow
summary: Learn why autonomous medical coding and CDI must work together to identify documentation gaps, improve coding accuracy, and reduce denial risk.
body_markdown:
Medical coding asks, “What does the documentation support?”


Clinical documentation improvement (CDI) asks, “Does the documentation completely and accurately represent the care delivered?”


A connected workflow answers both questions before billing.


The American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) emphasizes that complete, consistent[clinical documentation is essential to accurate coding](https://www.ahima.org/advocacy/policy-statements/data-quality-and-integrity/) , quality reporting, and appropriate reimbursement.


Yet[autonomous medical coding](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/autonomous-medical-coding-guide) and CDI are often evaluated as separate functions: one for coding productivity, the other for documentation quality.


The problem is that a coding system can accurately assign codes from an incomplete record and still miss a legitimate billing opportunity.


This is why **autonomous medical coding and CDI should operate as one connected workflow** rather than separate processes that identify and resolve documentation problems at different stages of the revenue cycle.

## What Is the Relationship Between Autonomous Medical Coding and CDI?


Autonomous medical coding assigns codes based on documented clinical evidence, while[clinical documentation improvement (CDI)](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/clinical-documentation-improvement-software) identifies missing, ambiguous, or inconsistent information that may affect those codes. When integrated, CDI evaluates documentation sufficiency during autonomous coding, helping the platform produce complete, accurate, and defensible coding decisions before billing.


The two functions have distinct but complementary responsibilities:


**Autonomous medical coding**


**Clinical documentation improvement (CDI)**


Analyzes clinical documentation to identify diagnoses and billable services


Evaluates whether documentation completely and accurately reflects the care delivered


Assigns ICD-10-CM, CPT, HCPCS, E/M codes, and modifiers


Identifies missing, ambiguous, or contradictory clinical information


Applies coding guidelines and applicable payer requirements


Identifies documentation gaps that may affect coding or medical necessity


Determines which codes the existing documentation supports


Determines whether provider clarification or documentation education is needed


Produces explainable coding decisions


Strengthens the clinical evidence supporting those decisions


> CombineHealth is built on exactly this integration. Its autonomous coding and AI-powered CDI run as one workflow: as it reads the encounter and assigns codes, it simultaneously evaluates whether the documentation supports them — so both questions above are answered together, before billing, rather than in separate coding and CDI queues.


## Why Does Autonomous Medical Coding Need CDI Inside the Workflow?


Autonomous coding needs integrated CDI because missing documentation can affect code specificity,[E/M levels](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/e-m-coding-guide) , medical necessity, and reimbursement. Identifying these deficiencies during coding helps prevent unsupported decisions, missed coding opportunities, and unnecessary rework.


Three problems make the integration important:


### 1. Autonomous Coding Cannot Assign Codes Without Supporting Documentation


[Autonomous medical coding systems](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/autonomous-medical-coding-services-usa) can identify diagnoses and services documented in the clinical record. However, they should not invent missing clinical facts to assign more specific codes.


For example, an orthopedic encounter may document a fracture without the laterality or encounter details required for specific code selection.


Integrated CDI identifies the missing information so the encounter can be evaluated for clarification.


The official ICD-10-CM guidelines require coding based on appropriate provider documentation and applicable classification rules.


> This is why CombineHealth evaluates documentation sufficiency as it codes. It assigns the codes the record supports, flags the missing specificity or evidence that would otherwise cause undercoding or an unsupported decision, and does it during coding, not after a denial, so documentation gaps are caught before the encounter is finalized rather than becoming a rework cycle. It never assigns codes the documentation doesn't support.


### 2. Accurate Coding Can Still Miss Reimbursement Opportunities


A system may correctly code everything documented in an encounter while missing services that were performed but insufficiently documented.


This can contribute to[undercoding](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-medical-coding-audit-uncovers-undercoding) , incomplete diagnosis specificity, and missed billable services.


Integrated CDI helps identify documentation deficiencies that may affect coding completeness before the encounter reaches billing.


Importantly, the goal is not to increase reimbursement regardless of clinical evidence. Any additional code or service must be supported by accurate documentation and applicable coding guidelines.


### 3. Separate Coding and CDI Workflows Create Unnecessary Handoffs


When coding and CDI operate independently, a documentation deficiency may be discovered after coding is completed.


The encounter may then require a CDI referral, provider clarification, and recoding.


An integrated workflow evaluates documentation sufficiency during coding, allowing supported encounters to proceed while material deficiencies are routed for clarification.


The benefit is not simply faster coding. It is reducing the risk of incomplete documentation becoming a finalized coding decision.


## How Should an Integrated Autonomous Coding and CDI Workflow Work?


A connected autonomous medical coding and CDI workflow should follow six steps:


1. **Review the complete encounter:** Analyze relevant clinical notes, diagnoses, procedures, medications, tests, and supporting records.
2. **Evaluate coding and documentation:** Identify supported diagnoses and services alongside missing, ambiguous, or contradictory information.
3. **Apply coding and payer requirements:** Evaluate official coding guidelines, medical-necessity criteria, and applicable configured payer rules.
4. **Determine the CDI response:** Finalize supported coding, record a documentation alert, or route the encounter for clarification.
5. **Produce**[explainable coding output](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/explainability-in-ai-medical-coding) **:** Link assigned codes and documentation findings to clinical evidence and applicable guidance.
6. **Analyze claim outcomes:** Identify recurring denial and reimbursement patterns that may warrant validated changes to future coding or CDI checks.


> CombineHealth runs this six-step workflow end to end: it reviews the complete encounter, evaluates coding and documentation together, applies coding guidelines and payer requirements, determines the CDI response, produces an explainable output that links codes and documentation findings to the clinical evidence, and learns from downstream claim outcomes to refine future coding and CDI checks.


## What Is the Difference Between a CDI Alert and a CDI Query?


A CDI alert identifies a documentation improvement opportunity that does not necessarily require the encounter to be held. A[CDI query](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/cdi-query-vs-alert) requests provider clarification when missing or conflicting information may materially affect coding.


**CDI alert**


**CDI query**


Supports provider education


Requests clarification from the provider


May not affect the current coding decision


May materially affect code selection


Can be tracked without delaying billing


May require holding the encounter


Identifies recurring documentation patterns


Addresses a specific documentation deficiency


> CombineHealth applies this distinction as it codes: lower-risk documentation patterns are recorded as CDI alerts for provider education, while missing or conflicting information that materially affects code selection is raised as a CDI query — so routine education doesn't interrupt billing, but a material deficiency is surfaced for clarification before the code is finalized.


## When Should an Encounter Be Held for Clarification?


An encounter can proceed when the existing documentation supports a defensible coding decision. It should be considered for clarification when missing or contradictory information could materially affect code selection, medical necessity, or compliance.


An integrated CDI and autonomous medical coding workflow supports two approaches:


### Code Now and Educate Later


The platform finalizes supported coding while tracking lower-risk documentation opportunities for future provider education.


This is appropriate when the missing information does not materially affect the current billing decision.


### Hold and Query


The encounter is routed for clarification when a material documentation deficiency prevents a defensible coding decision.


This may involve conflicting diagnoses, missing required specificity, or insufficient evidence supporting a reported service.


There should not be one universal threshold for every organization. The appropriate workflow depends on specialty, compliance requirements, and the significance of the documentation gap.


## How Does Explainability Connect Autonomous Medical Coding and CDI?


Explainability connects autonomous medical coding and CDI by showing the clinical evidence behind each code, identifying missing documentation, and explaining why an encounter can proceed or requires clarification. This gives coding, CDI, and compliance teams a shared basis for reviewing decisions and resolving disagreements.


An explainable workflow should make the following information accessible:


- Documentation reviewed and clinical evidence identified.
- Codes assigned and applicable coding guidelines.
- E/M rationale, where relevant.
- Documentation deficiencies requiring attention.
- Final coding, alert, or query decision.
- [Audit trail](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-audit-trail-work-for-medical-coding) of the review.


> CombineHealth makes all of this accessible on every encounter. That shared, explainable record is what lets coding, CDI, and compliance teams validate a decision and resolve disagreements — especially when the AI flags a documentation issue that affects the final code.


Explainability is especially important when AI identifies a documentation issue that may affect the final diagnosis or code.


## How Does Integrated CDI Help Prevent Coding-Related Denials?


Integrated CDI helps reduce documentation-related denial risk by identifying missing evidence, unsupported services, and medical-necessity gaps before claim submission. When combined with coding and payer-aware validation, it helps organizations address potential billing problems earlier rather than discovering them after adjudication.


Documentation issues can affect whether a claim satisfies applicable coverage and coding requirements.

## How Claim Outcomes Improve Autonomous Coding and CDI?


Claim outcomes can reveal recurring coding, documentation, and payer-related problems that were not apparent before submission. A self-learning platform can analyze denials, reimbursements, and underpayments to identify patterns, propose improvements, and apply validated changes to future coding and CDI checks.


A connected feedback process should:


1. Identify recurring denial or reimbursement patterns.
2. Determine whether the cause involves coding, documentation, coverage, or payer adjudication.
3. Propose the appropriate coding, CDI, or validation change.
4. Review and test the proposed change.
5. Apply validated updates and monitor subsequent outcomes.

## FAQs


### **Can autonomous medical coding work without CDI?**


Yes. Autonomous coding can assign codes from available documentation, but incomplete records may limit coding specificity or completeness. Integrated CDI identifies documentation deficiencies during coding and helps determine whether clarification is required before finalizing the encounter.


### **Is CDI the same as autonomous medical coding?**


No. Autonomous coding assigns codes based on documented diagnoses and services. CDI evaluates whether the documentation accurately and completely represents the care delivered. Integrating them allows documentation sufficiency and coding decisions to be evaluated together.


### **Can CombineHealth audit existing EHR-generated codes?**


Yes. CombineHealth supports an audit workflow that evaluates existing codes against clinical documentation and applicable requirements. It can identify unsupported selections, potential missed coding opportunities, and documentation gaps without requiring organizations to replace their existing coding process.


### **How does CombineHealth integrate CDI into autonomous medical coding?**


CombineHealth evaluates documentation completeness during autonomous coding rather than treating CDI as a separate process. It identifies missing or conflicting clinical information, applies coding guidelines, and determines whether an encounter can proceed or requires clarification before finalizing the coding decision.
